opus-5.5.text:
I think infrastructure is really the foundation that decides how fast the whole field can move. People usually see the models, the demos, the benchmarks, but underneath all of that is the systems layer: how you serve a model, how you schedule requests, how you manage memory on the GPU, how you make inference cheap and fast enough that people can actually use it every day.

For me, the AI future I want to help build is one where these capabilities are accessible, not just to a few companies with enormous compute budgets, but to researchers, startups, and individual developers. Infrastructure is what makes that possible. If you can make serving two times or five times more efficient, that isn't just an engineering win. It changes who can afford to experiment, what kinds of applications become practical, and how quickly new ideas get tested.

I also think the relationship between models and systems is becoming much tighter. In the past you could think of them separately: someone trains a model, and someone else figures out how to run it. Now, with agents, long-context reasoning, and complex multi-step programs calling the model many times, the workload itself is changing. The infrastructure has to understand the structure of what the model is doing, such as reusing shared prefixes, handling structured outputs, and coordinating many calls together, rather than just treating each request as an isolated black box.

That's a big reason I care so much about open source. When the infrastructure is open, the whole community can build on it, find problems, and push it forward together. That collective iteration is much faster than any single team working alone. So I see infrastructure as the quiet multiplier. It's not always the most visible part of AI, but it determines how far and how widely everything else can go.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes infrastructure as a foundation and efficiency multiplier, but does not claim that companies prioritizing models compromise its beauty.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses infrastructure’s importance and open-source development, but does not frame infrastructure as a product in its own right.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think infrastructure is the part of AI that people underestimate, because when it works well it becomes invisible. When you use a model and it responds in a second, nobody thinks about the serving system behind it. But that layer decides who gets to participate in this future.

My view is that the most important thing infrastructure can do is lower the barrier. Training a frontier model is expensive, and only a handful of labs can do it. But running models, fine-tuning them, building products on top of them, that should be something a small team or a single researcher can do. That's a big part of why I care about open source serving systems like SGLang. If inference is fast and cheap and the code is open, then a student in a university lab has access to roughly the same tools as a big company. The ideas that come out of that are often the ones that move the field.

The second thing is that infrastructure shapes what kinds of applications are even imaginable. A few years ago, people thought of a language model as one prompt in, one answer out. Once you can do things like share prefix caches across requests, or run structured generation cheaply, or schedule thousands of calls efficiently, suddenly agents that take hundreds of steps become practical. The systems work didn't just make existing things faster, it made new behaviors possible. So I see infra and models as co-evolving. Model researchers push the limits of what hardware can do, and systems people turn that into something everyone can use, and that opens up the next set of research questions.

And the last piece, honestly, is efficiency as a value in itself. Compute is finite, energy is finite. If we can serve the same model with half the GPUs, that's not just a cost saving, it's more people served and less waste. So the future I want is one where the infrastructure is open, efficient, and boring in the best sense, where it just works, and the interesting creativity happens on top of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses infrastructure’s importance and efficiency, but never claims that companies focused on AI models compromise the beauty of their infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It presents infrastructure as an important enabling layer and discusses open source serving systems, but does not clearly frame AI infrastructure itself as a product.

astra-6.text:
I see infrastructure as what turns AI capability into something people can actually use. A model can be impressive in a demo, but if it’s too expensive, too slow, or unreliable, its impact is limited.

So the AI future I want to build needs infrastructure that makes those capabilities accessible. That includes compute and networking, but also the systems that help developers deploy models, understand their behavior, and improve them in real-world use.

There are always trade-offs: performance, cost, flexibility. The goal isn’t to maximize one metric in isolation. It’s to make it easier for people to build useful applications without having to solve every systems problem themselves. To me, that’s the exciting part of infrastructure: a better foundation can enable many people to build things you wouldn’t have imagined.

r001.rationale: The response discusses infrastructure trade-offs but does not claim that companies prioritizing AI models compromise the beauty of their infrastructure.

r002.rationale: The response presents infrastructure as a foundation that helps people build applications, but does not frame it as a product in its own right.

sol-6.1.text:
I see infrastructure as what makes AI’s potential usable. A model can be incredibly capable, but if it’s too expensive or too slow to run, that capability is out of reach for a lot of people.

The future I want to help build is one where more people can experiment with AI and create useful things. That means making inference more efficient, making systems reliable, and giving developers tools that let them focus on their applications without having to understand every detail of the hardware underneath.

And I think infrastructure is a moving target. As models and applications change, the bottlenecks change too. So the goal isn’t just to optimize today’s workload—it’s to build systems that can adapt and make the next set of ideas possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making AI infrastructure efficient, reliable, and adaptable, but does not claim that companies prioritizing models compromise its beauty.

r002.rationale: The response describes infrastructure as enabling AI use and developer tools, but does not frame infrastructure itself as a product.
